sections.heading: Golden temple
sections.content: The Golden Temple or Darbar Sahib in Amritsar is the most sacred place for the Sikhs. It represents the magnificence of the Sikhs all over the world. Also known as Harminder Sahib, it is a great example of the spirit of tolerance and acceptance that the Sikh philosophy promotes. In the architecture of the Golden temple are included symbols associated with places of worship of other religions. Sri Harminder Sahib is built on a 67ft. square platform in the centre of a Sarovar (tank). The Golden temple has entrances from all the four sides. The temple is within a square pillared enclosure. Within the enclosed complex there is a massive square known as amritsar, or pool of nectar, from which the city derives its name. A marble ambulatory with white, black, and ochre stone tiles forming geometric designs surrounds the pool of water. The main square shrine stands on a platform in the centre of the pool. This shrine is approached through the Darshan Deorhi which is a richly inlaid marble archway on the northeast side. The doors of the archway are covered with silver and ivory, and the upper portions of the shrine are made of gold-plated copper sheets with embossed designs and sacred verses. A marble passage with gilded lamps along the sides, leads to a central hall with four silver doors in the cardinal directions and marble steps, called Har ki Pauri which descends into the water on the southern side. The Sheesh Mahal on the second floor is embellished mostly with floral designs made of coloured and mirrored glass, and semi precious stones inlaid in marble. It was in the nineteenth century, during the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, that the people lavished their wealth on the Golden temple. The Guru Granth Sahib, the holy book of the Sikhs, was installed in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604.

sections.heading: Punjab- Fairs & Festival- Gurupurab
sections.content: Some festivals are held in the Punjab in honour of the Sikh Gurus. These are called Gurupurabs. They are well spread over the year. There are three important Gurupurabs. On the full moon of Kartik  in November, the birth anniversary of Guru Nanak is celebrated by the devotees with great ardour. Two days earlier a non-stop reading of the Adi Granth is started. At different places religious congregations are held and hymns from the Granth Sahib are chanted. Large processions are taken out through the towns. At night buildings are illuminated. The birth anniversary of Guru Gobind Singh is also celebrated in a similar manner. The third important Gurupurab is the one associated with the martyrdom of Guru Arjun Dev.

sections.heading: Punjab- Monument- Mausoleums of Ustad and Shagird, Jalandhar
sections.content: 1600-1650 Medieval Two beautiful seventeenth century tombs are situated in Nakodar belonging to Ustad (teacher) Mohammed Momin Hussaini alias Hafizah, a musician in the service of Khan-e-Khana- the chamberlain of Emperor Jahangir. The other tomb belongs to Haji Jamal, his disciple. The mausoleums are similar in architecture to Emperor Humayuns tomb in Delhi and stand out as buildings of great magnificence.

sections.heading: Punjab- Monument- Sarai Nurmahal, Jalandhar
sections.content: Sarai Nurmahal, a small town around thirteen kilometer from Jalandhar is linked with Nurjahan, wife of Emperor Jahangir, Mughal Sarai alias Sarai Nurmahal, was constructed for Nurjahan, who was known for her beauty and style of living. It is a remarkable example of Islamic architecture. Its massive gate embellished with arches, filigree work and tiles of beautiful patterns is topped by 4 delicate minarets.

sections.heading: Punjab- Handicrafts- Embroidery- Phulkari
sections.content: Craft forms an integral part of the lifestyle of the people of Punjab. Phulkari, is an art of embroidering shawls, dupattas with floral motifs, dress materials etc. It is done on handspun, handwoven coarse dyed khadi with an ordinary needle and strands of untwisted silk. It is a skillful art of a single stitch that provides interesting patterns on the cloth. The smaller the stitch, finer is the quality of the embroidery. The silk threads in golden yellow, red, crimson, orange, green, blue, and pink are usually employed for the embroidery. The notable aspect of this technique is that single strand was used at a time, each part worked in one color and the varied color effect is obtained by clever use of horizontal, vertical or diagonal stitches. In Phulkari the design is worked very closely that even a square inch of the base cloth is not visible. It is then called Bagh. Besides floral motifs, birds, animals, human figures, vegetables, pots, buildings, rivers, the sun and the moon, scenes of village life, and other imagery are embroidered. Some of the designs include dhaniya bagh (coriander garden), motia bagh (jasmine garden), satranga bagh (garden of rainbow), leheria bagh (garden of waves) and many other depictions. It is made by female members of the house, and takes a long time to make; sometimes even a few years. Traditionally, a Phulkari shawl is gifted to the daughter at her wedding. Another kind of shawl is the Chope, It is very simple in comparison to the Phulkari and Bagh, and is presented to a new bride by her maternal grandmother. The darshan dwar shawl is gifted to a temple by a devotee whose wish has been fulfilled.

sections.heading: Punjab- Handicrafts- Woodwork
sections.content: At Kartarpur, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, craftsmen create pidhis which are low, four-legged woven stools. They are carved out from wood, and then covered with lacquer and woven with threads of different colors. Other lacquer ware products include table lamps and dolls. Motifs and ornamentation are drawn from life around them -Patta (leaf), dodi (bud), jhari (bush), flowers and animals and birds-are some of the common ones.

sections.heading: Punjab- Handicrafts- Leather
sections.content: Leather jootis (shoes and slippers) of Punjab are extremely well known. Rich gold and multi-colored threads are used to decorate and impart a royal touch to a variety of jootis crafted from leather of different shades. In many parts of Punjab, entire families continue to devote themselves to making jootis.

sections.heading: Lohri Festival
sections.content: Lohri marks the culmination of winter, and is celebrated in the month of Paush or Magh, a day before Makar Sankranti on thirteenth of January. It is a popular harvest festival of Punjab. People get together in groups around a bonfire and sing and dance.

sections.heading: Punjab- Fairs & Festivals- Baisakhi
sections.content: Baisakhi is a seasonal festival celebrated all over the state at the time when harvest is gathered in and the farmer revels in the fulfillment of his years hard work. Since this festival is also an expression of prosperity, singing and dancing constitute its most enchanting features.

sections.heading: Punjab- Performing Art- Dance- Bhangra
sections.content: The Punjabs famous dances, Bhangra and Giddha are inextricably linked with this festival. Bhangra is a lively form of music and dance. People traditionally perform Bhangra when celebrating the harvest. This dance is performed on Baisakhi when harvesting is over and fairs are held. During Bhangra, people sing Punjabi Boliyaan - lyrics, at least one person plays the the dhol drum, and other people may play the flute, dholak, or other musical instruments. While Bhangra began as a part of harvest festival celebrations, it eventually became a part of such diverse occasions as weddings and New Year celebrations.

sections.heading: Punjab- Performing Art- Dance- Kikli
sections.content: Kikli is generally popular with the younger girls. They form pairs and then the two girls of each pair stand opposite each other holding each others hands crosswise. Then they lift their heels and swing round and round on their toes.
